pairs.evidence: Plain uses old context(Logger) receivers and misses ambiguity. RAG uses context(users: UserService), type-based call-site matching and same-scope ambiguity; all three expected facts are covered.

Both explain common/platform/intermediate placement. Plain explicitly covers signature matching but adds unsupported fine-grained modifier rules. RAG stays closer to source text yet omits explicit signature matching. Neither dominates on both completeness and grounding.

Plain correctly says an existing class must already provide compatible members. RAG falsely limits actual typealias to name-only declarations and prescribes inheritance when expect has any members. Adding same-package guidance does not offset this core error.
RAG supplies the listed-exception/subclass restriction and CancellationException exception for suspend calls. Plain omits both and overgeneralizes unannotated-function termination.

Plain confuses direct Swift export with callbacks and proposes unsupported @SwiftAsync/-Xswift-async controls. RAG gives native async and try await correctly. Its Alpha statement is true in the complete source but not supported by cited chunk [2].

Both correctly recommend external with no Kotlin implementation; both miss part of the detailed declaration rules. RAG again retrieves Wasm neighbors instead of the designated Kotlin/JS section, adding an overbroad experimental-status claim. Plain adds unverified plugin-version guidance. No clear core-answer gain.
Plain wrongly exports a Kotlin class directly and invokes methods from JS. RAG uses JsReference, toJsReference(), opaque JS handles and exported helpers calling get(), matching the Wasm guide.

Plain says stable in 2.0.20 and introduced in 1.9.0; the source says introduced in 2.0.20 and stable in 2.4.0. RAG gives the correct stability release and V4/V7 exceptions, though it omits introduction history.
Both identify the lambda export feature. Plain claims it works by default; RAG includes the required -Xsuspend-lambda-exporting flag and documented @JsExport/async example.

Both identify Swift inheritance. RAG accurately names cross-language inheritance and includes interfaces alongside the open base class; plain adds an unsupported flag and stability/default speculation. Both omit passing the Swift implementation back into Kotlin.

summary: My review found **7 improvements, 1 regression, 1 mixed result and 1 largely unchanged result** with RAG. The strongest gains correct outdated context syntax, Swift export mapping, Wasm object handling, UUID stabilization and the required suspending-lambda export flag. RAG is not uniformly better: q12 invents a restriction on actual typealias despite citing sources. Citation labels all resolve, but some cited chunks do not support the full attached claim (notably q12 and the Alpha claim in q14). These are judgments about this one selected run against the saved corpus, not a general accuracy estimate.
